summary: Describes LISP, an experimental network-layer protocol that separates IP addresses into Endpoint Identifiers and Routing Locators. It requires no changes to host stacks or the Internet core and can be deployed gradually. It was replaced by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

plainLanguage.summary: Your name stays the same even when you move house. A lookup service tells people your current address, so mail still finds you wherever you are.

subtitle: An experiment that splits who a device is from where it is, using tunnels and a mapping lookup.

tldr.problem: One IP address is asked to say both who a device is and where it sits in the network. Routing wants addresses tied to topology, while managing devices wants addresses that never change when the topology does. The result is poor routing scalability as multihomed sites multiply.
tldr.mechanism: LISP gives hosts Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and routers Routing Locators (RLOCs). An Ingress Tunnel Router looks up the RLOC for a destination EID, wraps the packet in a UDP-based LISP header addressed to that RLOC, and an Egress Tunnel Router unwraps it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6830 is an Experimental specification that the RFC itself says is not recommended for deployment beyond experimental situations. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.

today: RFC 6830 is an Experimental RFC that has been obsoleted by RFC 9300 and RFC 9301, and it was updated by RFC 8113. Use those documents for the current LISP specification.

sections.title: Why Split Identity from Location
sections.content:
RFC 6830 describes the Locator/Identifier Separation Protocol (LISP). It was motivated by the October 2006 IAB Routing and Addressing Workshop, whose key conclusion was that Internet routing and addressing was not scaling well, partly because of the growing number of multihomed sites that cannot be covered by topology-based or provider-based aggregated prefixes.

The underlying observation is that a single address field used for both identity and location forces a conflict. For efficient routing the address must be assigned topologically. For easy management without renumbering after topology changes or mobility events, it must explicitly not be tied to topology.

LISP replaces the one address with two kinds of number. Routing Locators (RLOCs) are topologically assigned to attachment points and are used to route packets. Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) are assigned independently of topology and number the devices. Both are syntactically identical to IP addresses; only their use differs.

The RFC states that no changes are required to host protocol stacks or to the core of the Internet, and that LISP can be deployed incrementally without a flag day.
sections.plainLanguage: An address on a letter says both who you are and where you live, which is a problem when you move. LISP gives you a permanent name and looks up your current address separately.

sections.title: EIDs, RLOCs and Tunnel Routers
sections.content:
An EID is a 32-bit (IPv4) or 128-bit (IPv6) value used in the address fields of the innermost header. A host gets a destination EID the way it gets any destination address today, for example from a DNS lookup. EIDs MUST NOT be used as RLOCs. An RLOC is an IPv4 or IPv6 address of an Egress Tunnel Router, and it is the output of an EID-to-RLOC mapping lookup. One EID maps to one or more RLOCs.

Hosts keep working as they do today. Two kinds of router do the new work:

  • Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR): receives packets from site hosts, treats the destination as an EID, looks up the mapping and prepends an outer header with an RLOC as destination.
  • Egress Tunnel Router (ETR): accepts packets whose outer destination is one of its own RLOCs, strips the outer header and forwards on the inner one.

The RFC calls either one an xTR. Proxy-ITRs and Proxy-ETRs, defined in RFC 6832, act on behalf of non-LISP sites. The ITR keeps an on-demand EID-to-RLOC cache, which is separate from the distributed EID-to-RLOC database of all mappings.

The RFC allows a maximum of two LISP headers on a packet. The first is for location/identity separation at a site, and the second is for Traffic Engineering inside a service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The host just writes the friend's permanent name on the envelope. The post office at your street (the ITR) looks up the friend's real address and puts the envelope inside a bigger one. The post office at their end (the ETR) opens the big envelope.

sections.title: Following a Packet Through LISP
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example in which host1.abc.example.com opens a TCP connection to host2.xyz.example.com.

  1. The host does a DNS lookup, gets an address (the destination EID) and sends an ordinary IP packet that is forwarded to an ITR.
  2. The ITR needs an RLOC for that EID, so it sends a Map-Request. Map-Requests SHOULD be rate-limited. They travel over the underlying routing system or through a mapping database system.
  3. An ETR at the destination site matches the requested EID against its configured EID-prefixes. With no match the Map-Request is dropped. Otherwise it returns a Map-Reply.
  4. The ITR stores the mapping in its map-cache and prepends a LISP header to later packets, using an RLOC from the reply as the outer destination.
  5. The ETR receives the packets, checks the addresses, strips the LISP header and forwards to the destination host.

To avoid an immediate lookup in the reverse direction, an ETR MAY create a gleaned entry that maps the inner source EID to the outer source RLOC. Such an entry holds a single RLOC and is only stored and used for a few seconds, until a verifying Map-Request has been answered.
sections.plainLanguage: The first time, the post office has to ask a directory where your friend lives and writes it in a notebook. After that, it just reads the notebook.

sections.title: The LISP Data Header and Large Packets
sections.content:
A LISP-encapsulated packet is the inner header with the host's EIDs, preceded by an 8-octet LISP header, a UDP header and an outer IP header with RLOCs. The UDP destination port MUST be the IANA-assigned 4341, and the source port is chosen by the ITR from a hash of the inner 5-tuple. The UDP checksum SHOULD be sent as zero, and an ETR MUST accept packets with a zero checksum.

The first LISP header word carries flag bits: N (24-bit nonce present), L (Locator-Status-Bits in use), E (echo-nonce request), V (Map-Version present) and I (Instance ID present), then 3 reserved flag bits that MUST be zero on transmit. The Instance ID is a 24-bit value an ITR can copy in so overlapping private address spaces stay separate; an ETR uses it to pick the forwarding table.

Copying rules: the outer TTL SHOULD be copied from the inner on encapsulation, and the ECN field MUST be copied from inner to outer, and a congestion-experienced mark MUST be copied back on decapsulation.

Encapsulation makes packets bigger, so they may exceed the path MTU. The RFC describes a stateless approach, where the ITR splits a packet with DF clear into two equal-sized fragments, and a stateful approach, where the ITR records an effective MTU per locator in the map-cache from ICMP Too Big messages. When DF is set, or for IPv6, the ITR drops the packet and sends an ICMP Too Big to the source. All four combinations of IPv4 and IPv6 for inner and outer headers MUST be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The big envelope has its own little label with a few checkboxes on it. Sometimes the big envelope is too fat for the mail truck, so the post office either splits the letter in two or tells you to send smaller letters.

sections.title: Mapping Messages, Reachability and Changes
sections.content:
The control plane uses UDP port 4342. Message types are Map-Request (1), Map-Reply (2), Map-Register (3), Map-Notify (4) and Encapsulated Control Message (8). Map-Register and Map-Notify are used with a Map-Server, whose behaviour is in RFC 6833. Map-Register messages are authenticated, and implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-1-96.

Locator selection: the server side influences the choice of RLOC with Priority and Weight fields in Map-Replies. An RLOC with the R-bit set to 0 MUST NOT be used. The mapping system does not provide reachability, so ITRs use other methods: Locator-Status-Bits in received packets, ICMP unreachable messages, the echo-nonce algorithm (an ITR sets the N- and E-bits and watches for the nonce coming back) and RLOC-probing (periodic Map-Requests with the probe bit set, sent to a locator). The RFC notes RLOC-probing is robust but costs many control messages.

Changing mappings: since ETRs do not track who cached their mappings, the RFC offers three approaches. The clock sweep uses the default mapping TTL of 24 hours and counts TTLs down before a change. A Solicit-Map-Request (SMR) is a bit in a Map-Request that tells a remote ITR to refresh its cache. Database Map-Versioning carries version numbers in the header.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office phone book can go out of date. So there are ways to check that an address still works, and ways to tell everyone that an address has changed.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content:
The RFC says most security mechanisms are expected to be part of the mapping database service. For data-plane-triggered mappings, protection against ETR spoofing comes from route-returnability: a 24-bit nonce in the data header and a 64-bit nonce in control messages, together with ITRs accepting only solicited Map-Replies. Off-path attackers lack the nonce, while on-path attackers can do far worse, as in the current Internet. LISP does not rely on a PKI, because that would challenge its scalability goal.

Other points: implementations should rate-limit Map-Requests and Map-Replies against denial of service, cap map-cache size, and note that an ETR can claim a shorter prefix than it is responsible for, which the RFC leaves for future work. ITRs MUST verify the source address is an EID belonging to the site before encapsulation, and an ETR MUST drop a decapsulated datagram whose destination does not match its EID-prefixes.

The RFC does not address automated key management and lists open issues for further experiments. It also states that this specification is NOT RECOMMENDED for deployment beyond experimental situations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody can easily forge the reply from the directory because each question carries a secret number that must come back. The paper also admits it is only an experiment and some safety questions are not answered yet.

fields.name: flags
fields.desc: Reserved; zero on transmit, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Nonce/Map-Version
fields.desc: 24-bit nonce, or source and destination map versions.

fields.name: Instance ID/Locator-Status-Bits
fields.desc: Locator-Status-Bits, or a 24-bit Instance ID plus 8 status bits when I is set.

items.label: Map-Request
items.desc: Asks for the mapping of an EID.

items.label: Map-Reply
items.desc: Returns the RLOCs for an EID-prefix.

items.label: Map-Register
items.desc: An ETR registers its mappings with a Map-Server.

items.label: Encapsulated Control Message
items.desc: Carries control packets between xTRs and the mapping system.
